summary: Defines how one party pushes a Security Event Token (SET), a signed JSON Web Token describing a security event, to another party. The sender makes an HTTP POST over TLS to an endpoint the recipient runs, and the HTTP response tells the sender whether the event was accepted or rejected.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine dropping a sealed note into a friend's mailbox and getting a quick thumbs-up or thumbs-down back so you know they got it.

questions: how to deliver security event tokens over http
what is push based set delivery
what does http 202 mean for a set
what are security event token error codes
subtitle: How a sender hands a signed security event to a receiver with one HTTP POST over TLS, and gets a clear yes or no back.

tldr.problem: A Security Event Token (SET) describes something security-relevant, such as an account being disabled, and it has to reach the party that cares about it. RFC 8417 defines the token but not how to deliver it.
tldr.mechanism: The SET Transmitter sends an HTTP POST over TLS to an endpoint run by the SET Recipient, with the SET as the request body. The recipient answers 202 (Accepted) with an empty body, or 400 with a JSON error code.
tldr.outcome: Push delivery fits when the sender can make outbound requests and the receiver can host a TLS endpoint. RFC 8936 defines the poll-based alternative for the opposite arrangement.

facts.label: Failure response
facts.value: 400 (Bad Request) with JSON err and description

today: RFC 8935 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2020. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its poll-based counterpart is RFC 8936.

sections.title: Push Delivery of Security Events
sections.content:
RFC 8935 defines how a SET Transmitter delivers a Security Event Token (SET, defined in RFC 8417) to an intended SET Recipient using HTTP POST over TLS. It is one of two delivery methods; the other is the poll-based method in RFC 8936.

Push delivery is meant for cases where all of these hold: the transmitter can make outbound HTTP requests, the recipient can host a TLS-enabled HTTP endpoint the transmitter can reach, and both sides are willing to exchange data. In some scenarios either method works, and in others only one does.

Out of scope: how endpoint URLs, keys and limits such as buffer sizes are exchanged between the two parties. How SETs themselves are defined is left to RFC 8417.
sections.plainLanguage: Push is like a courier who walks your note to a friend's front door. It only works if the courier can walk out and your friend has a mailbox they can reach.

sections.title: The Transmission Request
sections.content:
To send a SET, the transmitter makes an HTTP POST to a TLS-enabled endpoint provided by the recipient. The Content-Type MUST be application/secevent+jwt and the Accept header MUST be application/json. The body MUST be the SET itself, written as a JSON Web Token (JWT).

The transmitter MAY add an Accept-Language header to say which languages it prefers for error messages. How the transmitter finds the endpoint is not defined and depends on the deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: The envelope has to be labelled as a security note, and the sender can say which language they would like any complaint to be written in.

sections.title: Validating and Acknowledging a SET
sections.content:
On receipt, the recipient SHALL check that it can parse the SET, that the SET is authentic (issued by the named issuer and, if signed, signed by that issuer's key), that the recipient is an intended audience, that the issuer is one it is willing to receive from, and that it will accept this SET from this transmitter. How it does these checks is out of scope.

Once the SET is validated and stored in a way that meets the recipient's own reliability needs, the recipient SHOULD respond right away. It SHOULD NOT do further processing before answering; extra work should run asynchronously so the transmitter is not left waiting.

On success the recipient SHALL answer 202 (Accepted) with an empty body. A transmitter MAY send the same SET more than once, and the recipient MUST respond as if it had not seen it before. The recipient MUST NOT rely on a retransmission once it has acknowledged a SET. The transmitter SHOULD NOT retransmit unless it suspects a recoverable failure such as a network outage, and SHOULD wait a suitable time before retrying.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver checks the note is readable, really from who it says, and meant for them. Then they say "got it" straight away and do the slow work later.

sections.title: Failure Responses and Error Codes
sections.content:
For general HTTP problems the recipient uses the normal HTTP status code. If it cannot parse, validate or authenticate the SET, it SHALL answer 400 (Bad Request) with Content-Type: application/json and a UTF-8 JSON body holding two members: err, a Security Event Token Error Code, and description, a human-readable explanation whose wording is up to the implementation.

The response MUST carry a Content-Language header. If the recipient can answer in several languages it SHOULD pick one using the transmitter's Accept-Language; otherwise it MUST use messages an English speaker can understand.

Error codes are registered with IANA and the set is extensible, so a transmitter may meet codes not listed here. The registry is meant for automated systems, so codes SHOULD identify classes of error that a machine could react to differently, for example by refreshing credentials and retrying.
sections.plainLanguage: If something is wrong, the receiver sends back a short note saying what kind of problem it was and explaining it in words a person can read.

sections.title: Authentication and Authorization
sections.content:
Delivery builds on HTTP over TLS and the standard HTTP authentication schemes. The TLS server certificate MUST be validated using DNS-ID and/or DANE. Whether a party may supply actionable SETs can be decided from the SET Issuer's identity, the transmitter's identity (perhaps with mutual TLS), or other authentication methods.

Because SETs are not commands, recipients are free to ignore SETs that do not interest them.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver checks the address really is theirs and who is knocking. A note is only information, so they can just ignore ones they do not care about.

sections.title: Delivery Reliability
sections.content:
How reliable delivery must be depends on the use case. The response gives the transmitter enough information to decide what to do next, but retrying everything is not wise: an invalid_request error points to a structural problem that will probably still be there on retry, while access_denied may be transient, for example if the transmitter refreshes expired credentials first.

A transmitter may not know whether a SET arrived, for instance if the network drops before the success response. The RFC leaves the choice to implementers: retransmit and favour guaranteed delivery, assume success and save resources, or park the SET in a dead letter queue for manual review. Implementers SHOULD weigh their reliability needs against the cost of retries.
sections.plainLanguage: If you do not hear back, you must decide: send the note again, assume it arrived, or set it aside for someone to look at. The right choice depends on how important the note is.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
SETs may carry sensitive data, including personally identifiable information, so transmitters and recipients MUST protect their confidentiality. TLS MUST be used. The endpoint MUST support at least TLS 1.2 and SHOULD support the newest suitable version, which the RFC names as TLS 1.3. The client MUST check the server certificate and the guidance in RFC 7525 MUST be followed. Some use cases also need the SET encrypted with JWE.

A recipient may face a denial-of-service attack in which many invalid SETs make it waste effort on cryptography that is bound to fail. Mitigations include authenticating transmitters, for example with mutual TLS, and rate-limiting offenders. Because TLS and HTTP context is usually lost when a SET is forwarded or stored, a recipient that needs to verify authenticity later SHOULD ensure SETs are signed with JWS.

On privacy, transmitters should target SETs to subscribers' real needs, and MUST have the right legal agreements and user consent in place before sharing personal information. Even subject identifiers can be sensitive. Appendix A keeps, as non-normative background, the considerations from earlier drafts that allowed unencrypted transport.
sections.plainLanguage: Notes can hold private things, so they travel in a locked tube, and the receiver should be ready for people who spam fake notes to tire them out.

messages.label: POST (application/secevent+jwt)
messages.note: The request body is the SET as a JWT.

messages.label: 400 Bad Request
messages.note: Instead of 202 if the SET cannot be parsed, validated or authenticated: JSON with err and description.

viz.caption: INITIAL SECURITY EVENT TOKEN ERROR CODES

items.label: Bad request body
items.desc: The body cannot be parsed as a SET, or the Event Payload does not match the event's definition.

items.label: Bad key
items.desc: A key used to encrypt or sign the SET is invalid or unacceptable (expired, revoked, failed certificate validation, etc.).

items.label: Bad issuer
items.desc: The SET Issuer is invalid for the recipient.

items.label: Bad audience
items.desc: The SET Audience does not correspond to the recipient.

items.label: Unauthenticated
items.desc: The recipient could not authenticate the transmitter.

items.label: Not authorized
items.desc: The transmitter is not authorized to transmit the SET to the recipient.
